Featured work · 0-to-1

MoneyMitr — an AI-guided finance operating system for India's first-time earners

Young Indian earners juggle a UPI app, a savings app, an investing app, and a notebook for everything else — none of it built for someone opening their first bank account. MoneyMitr consolidates payments, goal-based saving, investing, credit visibility, and an AI copilot into one product, built around a real persona: Joy Hopper, a 19-year-old intern receiving her first paycheck.

"Know where your money is, know what to do next, and get rewarded for doing it."

— MoneyMitr product philosophy

My role

Took the founding concept of an AI-powered personal finance app called "MoneyMitr", which I took from a blank page through problem framing, user research, MVP scoping, business model design, competitive & market analysis, assumption mapping and hypothesis design, and launch-readiness planning on my own. Every artifact below is mine, end to end.

Discovery MVP Scoping Business Modeling Competitive Strategy GTM & Launch Readiness
01 · Research

Where trust actually breaks down

A 15-respondent survey plus follow-up interviews (July 2026) with urban Indian earners aged 18–28, active on UPI. Small sample, treated honestly: a directional signal of validated needs, not a statistically robust study — the same discipline I'd want on any team I ran research for.

5.2/10
Average comfort letting AI read spending data
13/15
Want guided, step-by-step investing help
13/15
Likely to use an AI finance app that prioritizes user data safety
8/15
Still track money in a notebook or phone notes

"The issue is not non-availability but adherence and discipline to use & follow those apps… that comes only with real value."

— Interview respondent, on why finance apps get abandoned
H1Validated

First-time earners have a real knowledge gap — 12/15 rarely or never use investing features despite wanting guidance, and directly asked to be taught "from zero."

H2Partially validated

Payment apps nudge spending over awareness — respondents linked UPI to higher spend because "money doesn't go through our hand," but no one described apps hiding other features, so the framing itself wasn't directly tested.

Next step: follow-up interviews targeting H2.

H3Validated

No existing tool combines integrated tracking with a real spend-limit solution — 13/15 respondents rely on manual, low-tech tracking (notebook, phone notes, monthly bank statement review).

H4Inconclusive

Young earners avoid asking elders for advice because of criticism — the survey didn't ask this directly, and family only appeared as a source of traditional advice (FDs, LIC), not judgment.

Next step: a dedicated interview question before validating or dropping it.

02 · Strategy

Scoping the MVP, the business, and the competitive wedge

Seven modules made the cut for v1; five didn't. Every inclusion or deferral maps back to a specific survey signal — not intuition.

#MVP featureWhy it's in v1
1DashboardBalance, safe spending limit/day, goal progress — the one screen answering "where's my money," direct response to the manual-tracking pain point.
2Bank DetailsLink ≥1 account — foundational; every other module depends on it.
3Manage Your MoneyAuto income/expense recognition — replaces the manual notebook/statement habit 13/15 respondents described.
4PaymentLayer (QR only)Table-stakes UPI parity — skip investment/CIBIL shortcuts in v1.
5iAllocate (goal allocation)Create a goal, up to 3 dashboard widgets, live progress — matches the desire for step-by-step guidance.
6AI Financial Copilot (lightweight)Answers real questions ("Can I afford X?") from dashboard data only — validates AI comfort without needing investment data yet, to ship with visible consent framing.
7User Details + SettingsPermissions and notifications — necessary scaffolding, low build effort.
Deliberately deferred to post-MVP — and why
  • Investments Dashboard & free CIBIL score — low current usage (Q3), high build cost, needs data partnerships.
  • Rewards Center — a good retention loop, but not the core problem being solved.
  • Goal Auto-Funding — a natural v1.1 once manual goal creation is validated.
  • Financial Health Score — best built once real usage data exists to make the score meaningful.
  • Layoff Protection & Student Mode — real interest, but a preference signal, not demonstrated urgency; heavier builds better saved as v2 differentiators.
Business model

Two segments, one core promise

Segments

Newly-earning Indians aged 18–28, split into Segment A — already juggling apps/Excel, wants consolidation + AI insight — and Segment B — financially illiterate, needs investing and saving taught from zero. Additionally, unique user supporting features such as Student Mode & Layoff Protection Mode which extend the promise of better financial management through life.

Revenue model

Freemium subscription (core free; paid tier unlocks unlimited Copilot, Financial Health Score, Layoff Mode) + a merchant-funded Rewards Center + a flat referral fee to a partnered SEBI-RIA — deliberately consistent with a no-commission-push trust position, not yet finalized or unit-tested.

Competitive landscape

A real, well-funded field — with one gap still open

Jupiter Money, INDmoney, and Simplify Money (Kuber.AI) each leave a piece of the same gap unclosed: beginner investing literacy, an integrated goal-based daily spend limit, judgment-free reflection, and radically transparent AI, held together in one coherent product.

FactorJupiterINDmoneySimplify MoneyMoneyMitr
Beginner investing education✗ generic✗ power-user✓ explicit✓ core diff.
Auto expense tracking✓~ net-worth focus✓✓
Goal-based daily spend limit~ Pots only✗~ no daily limit✓ core diff.
Privacy-first, transparent AI✗ complaints~ shares w/ partners✓ no commissions✓ core diff.
Judgment-free reflection~ growth UX✗ data-heavy~ supportive✓ core diff.
Product breadth✓ full super-app✓~ narrower✗ deliberately narrow

Sourced comparison as of mid-2026 · full detail in Competitor Analysis.

India's AI-in-fintech market was estimated at about $690M in 2025, with growth of roughly 19% a year forecast to 2034 (IMARC). Competitors range from seed-stage startups to venture-backed players — a real, well-capitalized field, not an empty one.

Benchmarked against Monzo

The strongest full-stack player in this demographic still hasn't closed the gap

Monzo — 12M+ customers and a young customer base — is the closest global analogue. Even after a decade of execution, its Pots stop short of a live, goal-linked daily spend limit.

Offering strength, 1 (low) – 5 (high)
Monzo MoneyMitr (proposed)
Verdict

Conditionally yes. Infrastructure (555M UPI users), appetite (survey respondents rated their comfort letting AI read spending data at 5.2/10 — real, but conditional on privacy), and a twice-validated gap point to a real opening — but Monzo's own decade-long path to scale is the caution: this is a market ready for a narrow, well-executed wedge, not a green light to out-build Jupiter or INDmoney on breadth.

03 · Validation

Turning the riskiest assumptions into falsifiable tests

Every part of MoneyMitr rests on assumptions the survey was never designed to test. I mapped 13 of them by evidence and importance — six landed in the "leap of faith" quadrant. Five get a planned test with a real pass/fail threshold before another line of code gets written; A3 is explored as a design concept until beta data is in.

Assumption map — evidence vs. importance
A1Consolidation preferenceA2Copilot trustA3Spend limit behaviorA4Onboarding completionA5AdherenceA6Judgment-free UXA7Freemium convertsA8Merchant fundingA9LLM cost at scaleA10Organic growth scaleA11AA partnership termsA12Compliant CopilotA13Vendor-level accuracy
Leap of faith — tested first Validate opportunistically / monitor Assume true
A2 & A5 — Will people trust and keep using a conversational AI copilot?LLM-powered Copilot + beta
Planned test: a working Copilot prototype powered by a large language model (LLM), which answers testers' money questions based on its training, followed by a 4–6 week beta. The LLM provider will be chosen during the beta on cost, guardrails and data-handling terms. We believe a privacy-transparent Copilot will get first-time earners asking it money questions on their own, not just trying it once — and that explainable, life-stage-aware nudges will keep them past the novelty window. Pass if: ≥40% of testers send 3+ queries in week 1 and ≥20% still do in week 4; Day-30 return rate ≥25–30% against a weak 11–20% category benchmark.
A3 — Does a live daily spend limit actually change behavior?Design idea: home-screen widget
To keep the daily limit in view without opening the app, MoneyMitr could include a home-screen widget showing the user's safe-to-spend amount, overall iAllocate goal progress and one-tap access to the AI Copilot (see Product Snaps, 08). Whether it changes spending behavior will be measured in the closed beta.
A4 — Do users complete bank-linking, or abandon at the trust-sensitive moment?Moderated usability test
Planned test: a moderated usability test, to be run against the existing onboarding + bank-linking flow with 8–10 users matching the Joy Hopper persona. Pass if: ≥70% flow completion with no single step showing a disproportionate drop-off.
A7 — Will enough free users convert to cover per-user cost?Fake-door pricing test
Planned test: an "Upgrade to Premium — ₹99/month" paywall to be shown at a simulated free-tier cap, with clicks logged and no charge. Pass if: ≥5–8% click-through, with willingness-to-pay clearing the real AA + KYC + LLM cost floor.
A12 — Can the Copilot stay useful while staying strictly educational?Compliance audit + rating
Planned test: 15–20 realistic Copilot Q&As to be drafted, compliance-reviewed for anything crossing into personalized buy/sell advice, then usefulness-rated by the same testers. Pass if: ≥4/5 average usefulness, zero compliance-flagged responses.
04 · Go-to-market & launch readiness

A phased rollout, and the checklist behind it

Built against the product's real constraints: the mock-vs-real integration gaps still open in the MVP build, the licensing thresholds a fintech has to clear, and the six leap-of-faith assumptions above needing real results — not just a plan to test them — before a launch date gets set.

PhaseAudiencePrimary goal
Closed beta20–30 users from the existing survey/interview pool + referralsValidate the six leap-of-faith hypotheses under real conditions.
Soft launchSeed community — 1–2 campuses or early-career networksStress-test onboarding, account-linking, and support load at low volume.
Public launchOpen App Store / Play Store availabilityScale via organic + referral once soft-launch metrics clear their thresholds.
Pre-launch · to complete before launch
  • Live Account Aggregator integration signed & working
  • Real KYC/eKYC flow — no silent mocks in production
  • Data encrypted at rest & in transit, independently reviewed
  • DPDP Act obligations mapped: consent capture, audit trail, grievance contact
  • Legal read-through: Copilot stays "education," not "advice"
GTM launch
  • Messaging pressure-tested against both audience segments
  • Differentiation vs. Jupiter / INDmoney / Simplify explicit in copy
  • Analytics live on all four core health metrics before day one
  • Rollback plan for a critical issue in the first 48 hours
  • Go/no-go meeting — checklist reviewed line by line
Post-launch
  • Daily monitoring: signups, onboarding completion, crash rate
  • Day-30 retention tracked against the 11–20% category benchmark
  • Monthly compliance audit of real Copilot conversations
  • Win-back nudges for users inactive 14+ days
  • Quarterly refresh of the full assumption map
